name: Stamulumab

lead: Stamulumab (MYO-029) is a monoclonal antibody that binds myostatin, the protein that restrains muscle growth. Muscle-minded readers mention it as an early attempt at removing the body's growth brake for a fuller physique.

It binds myostatin in the blood so the protein cannot activate its receptor on muscle cells, which should allow more muscle growth. Wyeth tested it in a phase 1 study in healthy volunteers and a phase 1/2 trial in adults with several muscular dystrophies.

paras: It is not available. Wyeth announced on 11 March 2008 that it would stop developing it for muscular dystrophy, and no study has examined it for cosmetic muscle building.
Published sources reviewed do not detail its safety results. It is an unapproved, discontinued investigational antibody.

angle.text: Stamulumab is a discontinued antibody that binds myostatin to lift the body's brake on muscle growth, aimed at more muscle and a fuller physique. It was tested in muscular dystrophy rather than for physique, and development stopped in 2008.

lead: Stamulumab (MYO-029) is an experimental monoclonal antibody that binds myostatin, a protein that limits muscle growth. It was developed by Wyeth as a possible treatment for muscular dystrophy [1]. The idea behind its interest in physique circles is a chain: blocking myostatin removes a brake on muscle growth, which in animals produces visibly larger muscles [2][3].

It was tested in a phase 1 study in healthy volunteers and a phase 1/2 trial in adults with several muscular dystrophies [4][5][6]. Wyeth announced on 11 March 2008 that it would not continue developing it for muscular dystrophy [1]. It was never approved, and no study has examined it for cosmetic muscle building.

Bodybuilding forum members noticed the drug in 2008, when T Nation threads asked whether it was about to be released; the myostatin-blocking class remains on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list [7][8].

paras: Stamulumab binds myostatin so that it cannot signal through its receptor, removing a brake on muscle growth [1]. Myostatin (GDF-8) is a member of the TGF-beta family that negatively regulates skeletal muscle growth, inhibiting muscle stem cell proliferation and differentiation [9]. Myostatin was identified in 1997 by Se-Jin Lee and Alexandra McPherron, whose knockout mice had roughly twice the muscle of normal mice; the gene is also mutated in muscular Belgian Blue and Piedmontese cattle, and a German boy with mutations in both gene copies was reported in 2004 to be unusually strong [10].

A translational pharmacokinetic analysis published in 2016 combined data from mice, rats, monkeys and humans. It found a large potency difference between mice and monkeys, estimated human clearance at more than twice that of typical antibodies, and predicted that exposures at 10 mg/kg every two weeks would reach only about half the maximum effect seen in monkeys at peak and 10 percent at trough [2].

Wyeth tested the drug in Collegeville, Pennsylvania. A phase 1/2 multiple-ascending-dose trial ran from 2005 to 2006 in people with facioscapulohumeral, Becker and limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, and the results were published in Annals of Neurology in May 2008 [1][6]. Wyeth stated in March 2008 that it would pursue myostatin inhibition by other approaches [1]. Later myostatin-pathway candidates, such as soluble activin receptor constructs and follistatin gene delivery, were tested in animals and early human studies [10].

A phase 1 study (72 healthy participants, begun October 2004) evaluated safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics [4]. A phase 1/2 study (108 adults with Becker, facioscapulohumeral or limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, begun 2005) was completed [5].

The published phase 1/2 trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled, with 116 participants in dose-escalation cohorts of 1, 3, 10 and 30 mg/kg. The authors reported good safety and tolerability apart from cutaneous hypersensitivity at the 10 and 30 mg/kg doses, and the abstract states that no improvements were noted in the exploratory efficacy end points [6]. A separate analysis of single muscle fibers in six patients (five on MYO-029) saw improved fiber contractile properties in four of the five treated patients, although whole-muscle strength measurements did not improve [3].

Stamulumab drew interest on bodybuilding forums. In 2008 a T Nation thread titled 'Stamulumab Being Released' asked whether it was about to reach the market, and another titled 'Is MYO 029 For Real?' quoted the Wikipedia description of the drug [8]. A 2018 T Nation post on a lean-bulk stack wished for a way to inhibit myostatin and remarked that stamulumab 'was a hope' [8].

Myostatin inhibitors are banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and sports-drug-testing reviews list stamulumab-type antibodies among emerging substances for which detection methods are being developed [7][11][10]. Products sold online as 'myostatin blockers' are described by Wikipedia as fake [10].
